hypothesis: An adversary who compromised Windows hosts in this network stole credentials from them (MITRE ATT&CK tactic: Credential Access).

assessments.reason: Store Skype app restart; only a WerFault crash dump.
PsExec-delivered PyInstaller payload that dropped Rar/sdelete and harvested credential files.
Dropped archiver used to pack harvested credential files with password fGzq5yKw.
Dropped anti-forensics tool used to wipe Rar.exe and the archives.
Run by pbeesly's PowerShell and wrote a passwordsDB file.
Used with plaintext password to run python.exe on NASHUA.
Wiped dropped payload and archives on scranton.
Oddly named screen saver in ProgramData\victim run by explorer, later sdelete-wiped.
Compiled Add-Type payload DLLs for the hidden PowerShell loader.
Started by PowerShell with -verb runas elevation.
Rapid launches from cmd.exe after HKCU Folder shell open command writes.

frame.restated: An adversary with existing access to Windows hosts on this network is stealing credentials from those hosts.
frame.what_would_confirm: Observable evidence such as LSASS process memory access (e.g., via Mimikatz or procdump), suspicious access to SAM/SECURITY registry hives, use of Windows Credential Manager APIs, or anomalous authentication events indicating credential theft.
frame.what_would_refute: Absence of any credential dumping tool execution, no unauthorized access to LSASS or registry hives, and no anomalous credential-related events on the compromised Windows hosts.

verdict.rule: Confirmed if >=1 in-scope incident of verified malicious findings (confidence >= medium); Inconclusive if only suspicious incidents or coverage gaps; Refuted if full coverage and no malicious/suspicious finding

T1003.name: OS Credential Dumping
T1003.reason: No dumping utility, dump file or hive export found. The pbeesly intrusion on scranton/nashua used Sysinternals, Get-PrivateKeys, screen capture and 7z/Rar exfil staging, none of which touch credential stores.

T1003.001.name: LSASS Memory
T1003.001.reason: PowerShell LSASS handle 0x1000, no dump file.

T1003.002.name: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.reason: All SAM_ALIAS/SAM_SERVER/SAM_DOMAIN handle requests are made by lsass.exe itself as SYSTEM (SCRANTON$); no reg save or SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM hive file copies.

T1003.003.name: NTDS
T1003.003.reason: No ntds.dit file access, no vssadmin/diskshadow/ntdsutil command lines, and no shadow-copy or NTDS references in sysmon, security, powershell or windows.other.

T1003.004.name: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.reason: No lsadump/secrets command lines, no 4656/4663/4670 events on SECURITY Policy Secrets objects, and no LSA-secret references in PowerShell script blocks or windows.other messages.

T1003.005.name: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.reason: HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 writes on nashua are performed by lsass.exe itself (PID 728) as normal cached-credential maintenance; no external reader of the Cache key.

T1003.006.name: DCSync
T1003.006.reason: Only one 4662 on newyork by NEWYORK$ referencing DS-Replication GUIDs; no repeated Get-Changes/Get-Changes-All pattern and no drsuapi/lsadump/dcsync tooling.

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.reason: The only packet-capture activity observed is the signed Microsoft Azure Network Watcher agent on scranton.dmevals.local (Microsoft CoreXT, launched by services.exe/WindowsAzureGuestAgent.exe) running 'netsh trace start capture=yes' and toggling the Microsoft NDIS Capture service — legitimate platform diagnostics. No tcpdump/windump/wireshark/rawcap/pktmon, no pcap/npcap/winpcap driver loads, no promiscuous-mode or sniff-related command lines or PowerShell script blocks (all dedicated checks returned zero hits). The suspicious unsigned C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on nashua, pushed via PsExec with plaintext credentials, is not a sniffer: all 348 of its connections target a single destination 192.168.0.4:8443 (outbound C2-style), not promiscuous capture. Zeek does not overlap the Windows window and shows no ICMP conn records.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.reason: pbeesly's PowerShell session on scranton ran Get-PrivateKeys (certificate/private-key export), accesschk, screen capture and 7-Zip exfil staging; a hidden-window PowerShell (PID 2976) loaded from monkey.png opened LSASS with 0x1F3FFF/0x1FFFFF.

T1056.002.name: GUI Input Capture
T1056.002.reason: Invoke-ScreenCapture on scranton.dmevals.local (PID 3852, job PID 3544) loops capturing the virtual screen to random .bmp files in the user's Downloads folder.

T1056.003.name: Web Portal Capture
T1056.003.reason: No wwwroot/inetpub/login file writes, no w3wp/IIS process activity, no 4663 access to web content paths; zeek window does not overlap and shows no HTTP POSTs.

T1056.004.name: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.reason: Hidden, obfuscated PowerShell (PID 2976) requested full-access LSASS handles (0x1F3FFF, 0x1FFFFF) with an UNKNOWN call trace on scranton; no explicit hooking API or dump artefact observed, so intent is inferred.

T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.reason: Zero 4625/4771/4740 events in windows.security; the single 4776 credential validation (newyork, pbeesly, Error Code 0x0) succeeded. No authentication-failure or lockout pattern.

T1110.001.name: Password Guessing
T1110.001.reason: No 4625 failures and no password-bearing process command lines; only unrelated 'failed' system messages (crash dump init, PTR registration) in windows.other.

T1110.002.name: Password Cracking
T1110.002.reason: LSASS accesses are svchost/Azure telemetry/wininit with GrantedAccess 0x1000, and SAM 4656 handles come from lsass.exe itself; no wordlists, potfiles, hash/crack command lines or ConvertTo-SecureString script blocks. Certificate .pfx export by Get-PrivateKeys is key theft, not cracking.

T1110.003.name: Password Spraying
T1110.003.reason: No 4625 burst and no user-list tooling; the 4648 events are pbeesly re-using its own credentials via PSEXESVC on nashua and svchost on scranton (lateral movement, not spraying).

T1110.004.name: Credential Stuffing
T1110.004.reason: No failed logons at all, so no replay of stolen credential pairs; credential-related messages are benign Credential Guard config and SAM remote-call restriction notices.

T1111.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
T1111.reason: No MFA/smart-card/token interception artifacts. 4648 explicit-credential logons are pbeesly via PSEXESVC.exe/svchost.exe plus routine DWM-/UMFD-/machine accounts; the only type-10 logons are pbeesly from 172.18.39.2 (Negotiate). 'Credential' registry writes are Windows-default CredentialGuard/CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc entries by lsass.exe/services.exe, and windows.other only shows 'Credential Guard configuration: 0x0, 0'. LSASS accesses are dominated by svchost.exe/AntimalwareConfig.exe/WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe with a few powershell/wsmprovhost accesses consistent with generic credential access, not MFA interception. The host is nonetheless compromised by other activity (malicious .scr, hidden PowerShell IEX, csc.exe, sdelete, exfil script).

T1212.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
T1212.reason: Managed LSASS access, no protocol exploit.

T1539.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
T1539.reason: No browser cookie store access or theft. The only cookie-related events are benign: rundll32.exe davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie spawned by svchost.exe for the WebDAV share http://192.168.0.4/webdav on scranton.dmevals.local, and svchost.exe creating the WinINet INetCookies cache file. No Cookies/Login Data/Web Data/Local State files were touched, no PowerShell referenced cookies, and Sysmon process-access to Edge processes came only from legitimate system binaries. Malicious PowerShell (Invoke-Exfil/BeachCleanup/SeaDukeStage) exists on scranton but collects the Downloads folder, not session cookies.

T1552.001.name: Credentials In Files
T1552.001.reason: passwordsDB written; plaintext password on PsExec command line.

T1552.002.name: Credentials in Registry
T1552.002.reason: All 17 Password/Credential registry value sets came from svchost.exe, lsass.exe, services.exe and winlogon.exe performing normal Windows/IdentityCRL/CredentialGuard/service operations.

T1552.003.name: Shell History
T1552.003.reason: No ConsoleHost_history access in Sysmon process creation or Security 4663/4656/4658 object access.

T1552.004.name: Private Keys
T1552.004.reason: Private keys archived and sent to WebDAV.

T1552.006.name: Group Policy Preferences
T1552.006.reason: Two external hosts (10.0.1.4, 10.0.1.6) opened NEWYORK sysvol and read SecEdit\GptTmpl.inf on 2020-04-30; Windows-side GptTmpl.inf/gpt.ini writes are routine svchost Group Policy processing.

T1555.003.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
T1555.003.reason: No browser credential-store files, command lines, process handles or script text; only a .pfx certificate export and an unrelated INetCookies write were found.

T1555.005.name: Password Managers
T1555.005.reason: Zero hits for KeePass/1Password/Bitwarden/LastPass/kdbx across sysmon, security, powershell and other channels.

T1556.name: Modify Authentication Process
T1556.reason: Hidden PowerShell stager (bitmap-decoded IEX, HKLM Javasoft IEX, base64 -e child) plus reflective GetProcAddress/ReflectedDelegate loader on scranton; PowerShell.exe PID 2976 opened lsass with 0x1fffff and UNKNOWN call-trace frames.

T1556.001.name: Domain Controller Authentication
T1556.001.reason: wsmprovhost.exe (WinRM, user pbeesly) on nashua opened lsass with 0x1f3fff and UNKNOWN frames, but no DC authentication/directory modification (no 5136/4739/4657) was observed.

T1556.002.name: Password Filter DLL
T1556.002.reason: No System32 DLL drops, no Notification Packages/Password registry changes, no PasswordFilter references; only benign Microsoft cryptdll/samlib/samcli loads.

T1556.005.name: Reversible Encryption
T1556.005.reason: No 4739 events and no Set-ADUser/dsmod/Reversible command lines or script blocks.

T1556.006.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
T1556.006.reason: No 4739/5136/4738 events or MFA-related command lines.

T1556.007.name: Hybrid Identity
T1556.007.reason: dsregcmd.exe runs as SYSTEM under svchost with template args on all hosts; no 5136 changes and no Connect-MsolService/Connect-AzureAD script blocks.

T1556.008.name: Network Provider DLL
T1556.008.reason: No 4657 NetworkProvider/Credential registry changes and no NetworkProvider/New-ItemProperty script blocks.

T1557.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
T1557.reason: No interception evidence in any dataset; network logons are Kerberos with one NTLM logon, and the credential abuse seen (PsExec with plaintext password from scranton to NASHUA) is direct use, not AiTM.

T1557.001.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
T1557.001.reason: SMB sessions go only to the DC NEWYORK.dmevals.local (IPC$/SYSVOL), DNS/LLMNR-style lookups are routine, and no poisoning or relay tooling appears in PowerShell or registry events.

T1557.002.name: ARP Cache Poisoning
T1557.002.reason: MAC-to-IP mappings are stable; the dominant responder MAC 12:34:56:78:9a:bc is a lab placeholder, and no MAC claims multiple IPs or gateway changes.

T1557.003.name: DHCP Spoofing
T1557.003.reason: No DHCP event codes in windows.other, no ports 67/68 in Sysmon, and no dhcp log type in Zeek; nothing observed suggests DHCP spoofing.

T1558.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
T1558.reason: Credential access is real (PowerShell/wsmprovhost opening lsass.exe with 0x1fffff/0x1f3fff on scranton and nashua, Get-PrivateKeys .pfx export by pbeesly), but no Kerberos ticket theft or forging artefact was found.

T1558.001.name: Golden Ticket
T1558.001.reason: krbtgt 4769 requests are ordinary renewable TGT renewals (TicketOptions 0x60810010, AES 0x12, status 0x0); no golden-ticket tooling or anomalous privileged logons.

T1558.002.name: Silver Ticket
T1558.002.reason: Service tickets are KDC-issued (4769, status 0x0) for machine accounts from 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6, matching the observed WinRM/PSEXEC movement; no forged service-ticket indicators.

T1558.003.name: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.reason: All 28 TGS requests use AES 0x12 (no RC4 0x17), no SPN request burst, and no Kerberoast/Rubeus strings in PowerShell script blocks.

T1558.004.name: AS-REP Roasting
T1558.004.reason: No AS-REP/GetNPUsers/DontRequirePreAuth strings in PowerShell and no Kerberos pre-auth failure burst in the security log.

T1606.name: Forge Web Credentials
T1606.reason: No cookie or SAML token forgery artifacts in any dataset. Zeek window (2020-04-30) does not overlap the Windows window and shows only ordinary ssl/http/kerberos traffic; no PowerShell script block or process command line references cookie/token/SAML; 5857/5858 hits are routine SYSTEM RSOP WMI deletes on newyork; logon-process stack shows no anomalous authentication package.

T1606.001.name: Web Cookies
T1606.001.reason: No browser cookie store was read, created or tampered with; the only cookie-path file creation is a benign LocalService INetCookies path written by svchost.exe on scranton. The malicious activity on scranton is LSASS credential theft (PowerShell PID 2976 opening lsass.exe with 0x1fffff/0x1f3fff) plus certificate export and WebDAV exfiltration, which is credential access but not web-cookie forgery.

T1606.002.name: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.reason: No SAML assertion/token forging observed: no SAML/Assertion/NotOnOrAfter script blocks, no saml/adfs/token HTTP URLs in Zeek, no token-minting tooling. Certificate private keys were exported to .pfx on scranton (Get-PrivateKeys/Export-PfxCertificate) and exfiltrated, which is certificate theft rather than SAML token forgery.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.reason: No MFA/2FA/authenticator push or prompt-generation activity in any dataset. The single hit set (C355, 85 events) is WMI 5857/5858 provider-start and RSOP DeleteInstance noise under SYSTEM/NETWORK SERVICE; windows.security has zero 4625 failures and only 4648/4776 explicit-credential and successful logons (pbeesly to NASHUA, PSEXESVC.exe); no mfa/2fa/authenticator/duo/okta/login strings in PowerShell script blocks, 4688 command lines or sysmon process creations; zeek (2020-04-30) does not overlap and has no login/auth/mfa HTTP URLs. hostui.exe execution on scranton is suspicious for other techniques but shows no MFA-prompt behaviour.

checks.purpose: Stack all process creations to spot credential-dumping tools (mimikatz, procdump, comsvcs.dll rundll32) among rare executables.
Stack process-access targets to find LSASS or other credential-store processes being opened.
Stack object types accessed under handle/object-access auditing to find SAM/SECURITY/LSASS objects.
Stack newly created processes to spot dumping utilities launched on hosts.

args.query: event.code:4104 AND (powershell.script_block_text:*lsass* OR powershell.script_block_text:*mimikatz* OR powershell.script_block_text:*sekurlsa* OR powershell.script_block_text:*DumpCreds*)

checks.purpose: Find PowerShell script blocks referencing LSASS/credential-dumping APIs.
Look for credential-dumping references in other Windows event channels (service installs, VSS, etc.).
Stack granted-access masks on LSASS process opens to reveal memory-read access typical of dumping.
Read individual LSASS access events with source image and granted access.

Other Windows channels may log SMB/WebDAV-related activity tied to forced authentication.
Stack SMB destination ports in Zeek conn records to find outbound SMB connections from workstations (ATT&CK NSM source for T1187).

args.query: event.action:http AND (http.request.method:PROPFIND OR http.request.method:MOVE OR http.request.method:OPTIONS)

checks.purpose: WebDAV methods (PROPFIND/MOVE/OPTIONS) in HTTP requests are an ATT&CK-listed indicator of forced authentication.

findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly executed a malicious screen-saver (C:\ProgramData\victim\cod.3aka3.scr) from explorer.exe at 2020-05-02T02:55:56Z, which spawned cmd.exe and powershell.exe. The PowerShell toolkit (script blocks written to C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1 and readme.ps1) contains Invoke-Discovery (AV/firewall and group enumeration) and Invoke-Exfil. The same host also probed 192.168.0.4 on 445/139 (SMB) and 8443 (SSL) from 10.0.1.6. The 5140/5145 share-access hits in windows.security are benign domain baseline (SYSVOL/GPT.ini policy reads by machine accounts NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$, NASHUA$, UTICA$ and IPC$ samr lookups), not forced authentication.

findings.title: No SAML token forgery; certificate private keys were exported for theft, not used to mint tokens
findings.summary: No SAML token forging was observed: no 4104 script block contains SAML, Assertion or NotOnOrAfter, no process command line references saml/token/cert, and the Zeek window (2020-04-30, non-overlapping with the Windows window) has no saml/adfs/token HTTP URLs. What did occur on scranton.dmevals.local as DMEVALS\pbeesly is the theft of the raw material that token forgery would need: Get-PrivateKeys enumerated cert:\LocalMachine and exported every certificate with a thumbprint to password-protected .pfx files in Downloads (e.g. coyn5igj.3io.pfx at 2020-05-02T03:04:57), and the same session had already read LSASS with GrantedAccess 0x1fffff. The .pfx files were then bundled into OfficeSupplies.7z and pushed to \\192.168.0.4\webdav. This is certificate/credential theft (T1552.004/T1555 territory) rather than SAML token forgery, so the technique itself is not confirmed.

findings.title: No adversary network-sniffing tooling, capture driver or promiscuous-mode activity found
findings.summary: Hunting for T1040 across the Windows telemetry produced no attacker sniffing evidence. Process-creation stacks on all four hosts (windows.security 4688 and windows.sysmon event 1) contain no tcpdump/windump/wireshark/rawcap/pktmon, and the dedicated checks for pcap/sniff/promisc command lines, pcap/npcap/winpcap image loads (sysmon event 6) and PowerShell script blocks mentioning pcap/sniff/promiscuous all returned zero hits. The only capture-capable activity is the signed Azure Network Watcher/netsh trace stack on scranton (reported separately as benign). The suspicious python.exe on nashua is not a sniffer: all 348 of its network connections go to a single destination 192.168.0.4:8443, i.e. outbound C2-style traffic rather than promiscuous capture of other hosts' traffic. Zeek (2020-04-30) does not overlap the Windows window and shows no ICMP conn records, so it cannot corroborate or refute sniffing.

Searches for keylogging artefacts returned nothing: no process command line or PowerShell script block containing keylog/GetAsyncKeyState/SetWindowsHookEx, and no hook/MiniDump script content. The 470 process-access events to lsass/winlogon/explorer are dominated by svchost.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1000 (PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION) and by the PowerShell session's token enumeration; none show the low-level keyboard hook or keystroke-polling pattern of a keylogger. The screen-capture loop on scranton is GUI capture (T1056.002), not keystroke logging.

These are machine/user key containers generated by the crypto API when the processes ran; no .pem/.pfx/.key file reads or copies were found (the dedicated .pem/.pfx/.key searches returned zero hits).
findings.title: RSA key-container files created under Crypto\RSA are normal CNG key generation, not private-key theft
No browser credential-store access observed
findings.summary: No evidence of web-browser credential theft. Searches for Login Data / logins.json / key3.db / key4.db / Cookies file creation in sysmon (event 11) returned only two unrelated files: C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx written by powershell.exe (a certificate export, not a browser store) and an INetCookies file under the LocalService ServiceProfiles warp package written by svchost.exe. The pre-supplied checks for browser-store command lines, file writes, browser process handles, object access and PowerShell script text all returned zero hits. The attacker's collection on scranton instead targeted documents/archives (Compress-Archive over *.doc,*.xls,*.pdf,*pass*,*login* etc.) and certificates, not browser databases.

findings.title: No Windows Credential Manager / vault / DPAPI access; LSASS handles from Azure guest agents are baseline
findings.summary: No Credential Manager harvesting was observed. There were no cmdkey/vaultcmd/rundll32 keymgr invocations (4688 command-line checks returned zero), no registry writes to Credentials keys (sysmon event 15 check returned zero), and no PowerShell script blocks referencing Credential/vault/cmdkey. The only 'credential' text in windows.other is a boot-time 'Credential Guard configuration: 0x0, 0' event on scranton. Object-access auditing on lsass.exe objects shows only baseline actors: C:\WindowsAzure\Packages\CollectGuestLogs.exe (0x1410/0x10) on nashua, utica, scranton and newyork, C:\Program Files\Windows Defender\MsMpEng.exe (0x1fffff) on scranton, and lsass.exe itself (0x1478). The pbeesly-attributed 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff handles from powershell.exe (scranton, 03:05:16) and wsmprovhost.exe (nashua, 03:09:29) are covered under T1555; the nashua one is explained by Get-Process -IncludeUserName. No vault/DPAPI secret extraction was found.

findings.title: No password-manager artifacts (KeePass/1Password/Bitwarden/LastPass) observed
findings.summary: All password-manager checks returned zero hits across sysmon process creation, file creation, process handles, security 4688 command lines, PowerShell 4104 script text and windows.other messages. No .kdbx files, no password-manager executables and no password-manager process access appear in the 02:55-03:28Z window on any of the four hosts. The only credential-like material the intruder handled was a certificate exported to C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx by powershell.exe on scranton at 03:04:57Z, which is not a password-manager store.

No writes of DLLs into System32, no 4657 registry changes under Notification Packages/Password/lsass keys, and no 4688/4104 references to Notification Packages or PasswordFilter were found. The only DLL loads near authentication components were ordinary Microsoft modules (cryptdll.dll, samlib.dll, samcli.dll) loaded by SearchProtocolHost/SearchFilterHost/WmiPrvSE/powershell, which is normal Windows behaviour.
findings.title: No password filter DLL installation observed

findings.summary: No 4739 policy-change events, no Set-ADUser/dsmod/Reversible command lines in 4688 or Sysmon process creation, and no PowerShell script blocks referencing AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption. The only account-related PowerShell activity was the malicious loader chain on scranton, which does not touch reversible encryption.
findings.title: No reversible-encryption / AD account flag changes observed

findings.summary: No 4739/5136/4738 events and no Set-ADUser/Set-ADAuthenticationPolicy style command lines were found in security, sysmon or other logs; nothing indicates MFA registration or policy tampering.
findings.title: No MFA modification observed

findings.summary: dsregcmd.exe ran as SYSTEM with the unexpanded template command line 'C:\windows\System32\dsregcmd.exe $(Arg0) $(Arg1) $(Arg2)' on scranton (03:19:12, 03:21:48, 03:24:13), newyork (03:06:14) and nashua (03:25:30), parent svchost.exe, and only loaded cryptdll.dll. No 5136 directory changes and no Connect-MsolService/Connect-AzureAD script blocks were found, so there is no evidence of federated-identity or token-signing modification.
findings.title: dsregcmd executions are routine device-registration checks, not hybrid-identity tampering

findings.summary: No 4657 registry changes under NetworkProvider/Credential keys and no PowerShell script blocks referencing NetworkProvider or New-ItemProperty were found; the malicious PowerShell on scranton used reflective loading, not a network provider DLL registration.
findings.title: No network provider DLL registration observed
No adversary-in-the-middle positioning observed; credential theft in this window used direct PsExec with plaintext credentials
findings.summary: Across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.other and windows.powershell (2020-05-02 02:55-03:28Z) there is no evidence of traffic interception. All network logons are Kerberos (123 NEWYORK$, 37 SCRANTON$, 25 NASHUA$, 19 pbeesly, 8 WEC$, 5 UTICA$) with a single NTLM logon (pbeesly, logon type 3, from 172.18.39.2 to scranton at 03:20:41). Sysmon event 3 destinations are the normal DC/file-server ports (445, 389, 88, 53, 135) and all DestinationHostname values are '-'. The actual intrusion in this window is direct: pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local ran PsExec64.exe against \\NASHUA with the password supplied on the command line, and installed a javamtsup service on scranton. That is credential use, not credential interception, so T1557 itself is not supported.

findings.title: SMB traffic and name resolution are normal; no LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning or SMB relay artifacts
findings.summary: Zeek (2020-04-30 00:06-00:45Z) shows only ordinary SMB to the domain controller NEWYORK.dmevals.local (10.0.0.4): IPC$ pipe mappings, SYSVOL GPO reads (gpt.ini, GptTmpl.inf) and krb,smb,gssapi sessions from 10.0.1.4 and 10.0.1.6. No SMB session is directed at an unauthorized host and no relay-style authentication to a non-DC endpoint appears. DNS queries are routine (wpad.dmevals.local, wec.dmevals.local, _ldap._tcp SRV lookups, Microsoft telemetry); the only name-resolution oddities are single 'wpad' and 'prisoner.iana.org' lookups, which are standard Windows/connectivity-test behaviour. Sysmon 22 query names on the Windows hosts are likewise normal (host names, _ldap._tcp SRV records, Microsoft domains). No PowerShell script block references LLMNR, NBT-NS, Responder or relay tooling, and no 4657 DNS client registry tampering was found.

findings.title: No ARP cache poisoning: MAC-to-IP mappings are stable and the responder MAC is a lab placeholder
findings.summary: Zeek conn records show only three source MACs (00:0d:3a:13:e3:69, 00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2, fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1) and two responder MACs (12:34:56:78:9a:bc, 00:0d:3a:13:e3:69) plus broadcast. The dominant responder MAC 12:34:56:78:9a:bc is a well-known synthetic/placeholder address used in lab captures and is consistently paired with the internal hosts 10.0.0.4 and 10.0.1.6; no single MAC is seen claiming multiple unrelated IPs in a way that indicates gratuitous-ARP spoofing, and no duplicate-IP conflict or gateway MAC change appears. No PowerShell script block references arp or netsh interface manipulation. The only network anomalies are Zeek 'weird' events (ip_hdr_len_zero, truncated_IP, unknown_dce_rpc_auth_type) and two self-signed-certificate SSL notices, which are capture/validation artifacts rather than poisoning.

findings.title: No golden-ticket evidence: krbtgt TGS requests are ordinary TGT renewals, all tickets AES (0x12)
findings.summary: All 28 event 4769 on newyork.dmevals.local have TicketEncryptionType 0x12 and Status 0x0. The two krbtgt service-ticket requests (03:04:04 by pbeesly@DMEVALS.LOCAL, 03:19:13/03:19:15 by SCRANTON$@DMEVALS.LOCAL) carry TicketOptions 0x60810010 (renewable/renew) and come from 10.0.1.4, i.e. normal TGT renewal traffic, not forged-ticket use. No 4672 special-privilege logons could be attributed to unusual principals (aggregation returned no buckets), no krbtgt/golden keywords in PowerShell script blocks, and no DC-side Kerberos events exist in windows.other. The LSASS access by PowerShell on scranton is credential dumping, but nothing shows a forged TGT being used.

findings.title: No silver-ticket evidence: service tickets are machine-account TGS requests from 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6
findings.summary: The 4769 service tickets on newyork.dmevals.local target NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$ and WEC$ and are requested by pbeesly@DMEVALS.LOCAL and SCRANTON$@DMEVALS.LOCAL from 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6, all with Status 0x0 and AES encryption 0x12 — consistent with the observed WinRM/PSEXEC lateral movement, not with forged service tickets (which would not generate KDC 4769 events at all). No 'silver'/SPN tooling in PowerShell script blocks.

findings.title: No Kerberoasting: no RC4 service-ticket bursts or roasting tooling
findings.summary: No 4769 event has TicketEncryptionType 0x17 (RC4) — all 28 are 0x12 — and there is no burst of service-ticket requests for user/service SPNs. PowerShell script blocks contain no Kerberoast/Invoke-Kerberoast/Rubeus strings (zero hits), and the zeek Kerberos capture (2020-04-30, non-overlapping window) shows only 14 AS and 11 TGS requests. The credential access seen on scranton/nashua targeted LSASS and certificate private keys, not Kerberos service tickets.

findings.title: No AS-REP roasting: no pre-auth-disabled account enumeration or GetNPUsers activity
findings.summary: No PowerShell script block references AS-REP/asrep/GetNPUsers/DontRequirePreAuth (zero hits), and the security log contains no 4768/4771 Kerberos pre-authentication failure burst that would accompany AS-REP roasting. The only Kerberos activity is successful 4769 issuance on newyork.dmevals.local.

findings.title: No forged web credential (cookie/SAML) activity observed; instead a full credential-access and exfiltration chain on scranton.dmevals.local
findings.summary: Hunting for T1606 (forging web credentials) produced no evidence of cookie or SAML token forgery. The Zeek window (2020-04-30) does not overlap the Windows window (2020-05-02) and contains only ordinary ssl/http/kerberos log types with no saml/adfs/token URLs; no PowerShell 4104 script block mentions cookie, token, SAML, Assertion or NotOnOrAfter; no process command line references saml/token/cert; the only cookie-path file creation is a benign LocalService INetCookies path created by svchost.exe on scranton. The 5857/5858 WMI hits are routine RSOP_ExtensionStatus DeleteInstance operations by NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM on newyork, and the 4624/4648 logon-process stack (Kerberos 217, Advapi 76, User32 2, NtLmSsp 1) shows no anomalous authentication package. However, the same host does show a genuine credential-access intrusion (see T1606.001/T1606.002 findings) that is better described by other techniques.

findings.title: No MFA/2FA request-generation activity observed; only WMI provider noise and unrelated hostui.exe execution
findings.summary: Hunting for T1621 (Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation) across the 2020-05-02 02:55-03:28Z Windows window found no MFA-fatigue indicators. The only hit (check C355, 85 events) is Windows Management Instrumentation noise: event 5858 'Start IWbemServices::DeleteInstance - Root\Rsop\Computer : RSOP_ExtensionStatus...' (48 on newyork.dmevals.local, 1 on scranton) and event 5857 WMI provider-start messages (e.g. 'CIMWin32 provider started with result code 0x0. HostProcess = wmiprvse.exe'), all under SYSTEM/NETWORK SERVICE/LOCAL SERVICE - routine RSOP/WMI provider lifecycle, not authentication. No 4625 failed logons exist in windows.security at all; the only authentication-adjacent events are 4648 explicit-credential logons by pbeesly from scranton.dmevals.local to NASHUA (10.0.1.6) and PSEXESVC.exe on nashua.dmevals.local, plus one successful 4776 (Status 0x0) for pbeesly on newyork - consistent with lateral movement tooling, not MFA push spam. No PowerShell script block or process command line in windows.powershell or windows.security 4688 contains mfa/2fa/authenticator/duo/okta/login strings. The only 'auth'-adjacent process is C:\Windows\System32\hostui.exe on scranton.dmevals.local, launched by pbeesly via 'Start-Process C:\Windows\System32\hostui.exe -verb runas' (PowerShell 4104, ScriptBlockId 07cee247-5933-49b5-a354-aa92f35c34c3) with a StartUp persistence shortcut hostui.lnk; this is a renamed/unsigned binary (Company/Description/OriginalFileName '-') but shows no MFA-prompt behaviour in the telemetry. Zeek data (2020-04-30) does not overlap the Windows window and contains no login/auth/mfa HTTP URLs. T1621 is therefore not observed in this data.

findings.title: Routine OS certificate-store maintenance by svchost/lsass/taskhostw and a single ROOT store blob update by Sysmon on nashua
findings.summary: The remaining certificate-related registry hits are normal Windows certificate-store maintenance, not certificate theft or forging. Sysmon event 13 writes under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\SystemCertificates were made by C:\windows\system32\svchost.exe (AuthRoot AutoUpdate DisallowedCertLastSyncTime and AuthRoot/Windows Live ID Token Issuer certificate blobs), C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe (AuthRoot certificate blob on nashua), C:\windows\system32\taskhostw.exe (per-user ACRS PhysicalStores settings on scranton) and C:\windows\System32\smss.exe (WOW6432Node SymbolicLinkValue). The single Security 4657 hit is a modification of the ROOT store value \REGISTRY\MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\ROOT\Certificates\BE36A4562FB2EE05DBB3D32323ADF445084ED656 (value 'Blob') on nashua.dmevals.local by NASHUA$ (S-1-5-18, logon 0x3E7) with process name C:\Windows\Sysmon.exe — a trusted-root store update consistent with normal certificate trust-list servicing, with no attacker tooling, no export and no private-key access. The 14 Kerberos 4768 TGT requests (pbeesly x9, SCRANTON$ x5) on newyork.dmevals.local are ordinary krbtgt ticket requests with no certificate/PKINIT indicators. Zeek x509 records (separate, non-overlapping 2020-04-30 window) contain only two self-signed subjects (rempel.group.net x376, conn.sons.info x2) on unrelated hosts, with no evidence of forged authentication certificates.

findings.title: No DHCP spoofing: no DHCP log source, no DHCP ports, no DHCP-related events
findings.summary: There is no DHCP telemetry to indicate rogue DHCP activity. The windows.other System channel contains no DHCP client/server event codes (1341/1342/1020/1063 absent from the 216 events), and no PowerShell script block mentions DHCP. Sysmon event 3 destination ports contain no 67/68 traffic; the only broadcast traffic is normal NetBIOS name service (137) and datagram (138) to 10.0.1.255 from scranton, nashua and utica. The Zeek capture has no dhcp log type at all (only conn, files, ssl, x509, dce_rpc, http, dns, kerberos, dpd, smb_files, weird, smb_mapping, notice, pe), so DHCP spoofing is not observable in this data and nothing observed suggests it.

incidents.title: Hidden PowerShell loader (monkey.png steganography) compiles Add-Type payloads and opens LSASS with full access on scranton
incidents.rationale: All describe the same LSASS-access action by PowerShell-family processes attributable to pbeesly: hidden PowerShell PID 2976 on scranton opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff and UNKNOWN call-trace frames, plus the lower-privilege 0x1000 opens and the wsmprovhost LSASS open on nashua. The csc.exe Add-Type compiles from the same hidden loader are part of this action chain. Best fit is LSASS Memory (T1003.001); no dump file was written, hence suspicious.

incidents.title: Hands-on-keyboard credential-access toolkit in pbeesly's PowerShell session on scranton (discovery, accesschk, private-key export, screen capture, exfil staging)
incidents.rationale: Single finding describing the combined hands-on-keyboard session; the umbrella Input Capture technique (T1056) is the best single fit for the session that includes screen capture and keystroke collection alongside other credential tooling.

incidents.title: Get-Keystrokes keylogger job on scranton
incidents.rationale: Get-Keystrokes background job launched, viewed and removed is keylogging.

incidents.title: Screen capture loop (Invoke-ScreenCapture) on scranton
incidents.rationale: Invoke-ScreenCapture background job writing .bmp screenshots of the desktop is GUI input capture.

incidents.title: WebDAV/UNC forced-authentication channel used to exfiltrate OfficeSupplies.7z to 192.168.0.4
incidents.rationale: Both describe the same Invoke-Exfil action mapping \\192.168.0.4\webdav and copying the archive; the WebDAV/UNC forced-authentication channel is T1187.

incidents.title: Credential-adjacent file harvesting and archiving on scranton and nashua
incidents.rationale: Both describe the same collection action: enumerating user files matching *pass*/*psw*/*login*/*admin*/*vpn* patterns and archiving them (Draft.Zip on scranton, working.zip on nashua).

incidents.title: Plaintext password on PsExec command line to NASHUA; accesschk passwordsDB on scranton
incidents.rationale: Both describe credentials in files/command lines: accesschk writing passwordsDB and PsExec64 run with '-p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by' against NASHUA.

incidents.title: Private keys packed into 7z and pushed to attacker WebDAV
incidents.rationale: Invoke-Exfil compressing Downloads containing the exported .pfx keys and copying to the WebDAV share is theft of private keys (T1552.004).

incidents.title: GptTmpl.inf read from NEWYORK sysvol by external hosts and GroupPolicy DataStore writes
incidents.rationale: Reading the SYSVOL security-template GptTmpl.inf is Group Policy Preferences credential access (T1552.006).

incidents.title: hostui.exe elevated via runas from PowerShell on scranton
incidents.rationale: Elevation via runas from PowerShell; assessed under Group Policy Preferences (T1552.006) at low confidence.

incidents.title: Get-PrivateKeys certificate export treated as credential-store access on scranton
incidents.rationale: Same Get-PrivateKeys action; grouped separately as the credential-store access characterization (T1555).

incidents.title: Get-PrivateKeys .pfx export characterized as Windows Credential Manager access
incidents.rationale: Same Get-PrivateKeys action; the finding characterizes it as credential-store access (T1555.004).

incidents.title: sdclt.exe UAC-bypass pattern preceding Add-Type compile on scranton
incidents.rationale: sdclt.exe launches following HKCU Folder shell open command writes; assessed as Modify Authentication Process (T1556) at low confidence.

incidents.title: No SAML token forgery; certificate private keys exported for theft
incidents.rationale: Finding explicitly reports no SAML token forging but the Get-PrivateKeys export; the observed action is certificate private-key theft, assessed under the SAML-token hypothesis as negative.

incidents.title: Certificate private-key export (Get-PrivateKeys) to .pfx on scranton
incidents.rationale: Same Get-PrivateKeys action exporting LocalMachine certificate private keys to password-protected .pfx files; best fit is Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates (T1649).
